paragraphs: The Guardian reports that the Democratic sweep of Congress in this week's US elections may make it easier for Israel's splintered opposition to overcome its divisions and form a coalition government. The paper says the result raises the urgency of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu, who has tied himself closely to Donald Trump's Republicans.

The opposition won 67 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, according to the Guardian. More than a quarter of those went to Palestinian citizens of Israel, and some Jewish opposition parties have ruled out sitting with them.

Opposition politician Yair Lapid said incoming Democratic lawmakers "aren't against Israel" but are mainly against Netanyahu. He proposed a charm offensive by officials of a prospective new government to rebuild trust. Brad Lander, a Democratic congressman-elect who calls himself a liberal Zionist, replied that Americans were not hungry for a tour but wanted "respect for international law and human rights". Lander and two other incoming Jewish members of Congress also wrote to Israel's ambassador asking for the release of journalist Abed Abu Shehada. His lawyers say interrogators have asked him only about a podcast interview. The Israeli response to the letter was not reported.

Republicans are also part of the picture. The Guardian says Vice President JD Vance listed the relationship with Israel among reasons for voter anger, and that Trump pledged on election day to cut $4bn in annual military aid. An Israeli official told Channel 12 the announcement caused panic in the defence establishment. Netanyahu's office said on Friday that the cut reflected a "move from aid to partnership".

Columnist Ben Caspit wrote in Ma'ariv that "we are losing America" and called it "a decree of Netanyahu". Nadav Tamir of J Street Israel wrote that outside pressure from supporters of Israel's security could push the country toward change. Whether the opposition can turn its Knesset seats into a government remains the open question.

Thomas Markle, the 82-year-old father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida. He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the US Department of Justice. A federal complaint alleges he held images showing child sex abuse. He has not been convicted.

At a 30-minute hearing on Friday he was ordered to submit to electronic monitoring. No plea was taken, and an arraignment date in California will be set later, the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office for Central California said. Markle appeared in a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. He has previously denied allegations of possessing such images, calling them "sick lies".

The case followed FBI searches of storage units in Los Angeles that Markle had rented since 2008, with the last payment made in October, the DoJ said. The FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that it alleges contained child sex abuse material. Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two images, and the man pictured appears to be in his 30s to 40s, which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades. FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly".

Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home there. Meghan's half brother, Thomas Markle Jr, handed four boxes of material to officers. Separately, London's Metropolitan Police confirmed it received a letter in 2019 making a "number of claims" about Markle. It passed the information to the Sussexes' office and has referred itself to the police conduct watchdog over its handling.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on the arrest. In October, Meghan said she was "deeply distressed" by the news. She has been estranged from her father since 2018.

Al Jazeera reports that Jean-Luc Melenchon, the 75-year-old leader of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party, has emerged as the strongest contender on the left ahead of next year's French presidential election. Right-wing opponents call him a "radical" and former allies a "despot", while some students in recent nationwide protests call him a "hero".

He presented his programme at a rally in Le Bourget on Saturday. It would lower the retirement age to 60, raise the minimum wage to 1,700 euro a month, withdraw France from NATO and renationalise parts of the economy. He also wants the European Central Bank to stop France repaying the debt it holds, turning it into a permanent interest-free loan. LFI says higher taxes on wealthy individuals and corporations would pay for the spending, including a minimum 2 percent tax on billionaires' wealth.

Critics question the numbers. Some economists warn his plans could lead investors to sell French government bonds, raising borrowing costs. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said in September that "borrowing money and deciding not to give it back" is "theft". Political analyst Beligh Nabli argued that the radical label is only relative, since LFI is one of the few parties still defending state intervention in the economy.

Polls this week put Melenchon at 17.5 to 18 percent, ahead of Raphael Glucksmann, who has Socialist Party backing. Glucksmann has ruled out supporting him, while other left parties are weighing it. Tensions also surround Melenchon's refusal to call Hamas a "terrorist organisation" and his accusation that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza. Political opponents on the left accuse him of fuelling anti-Semitism, which he rejects.
An October Toluna Harris Interactive poll found Marine Le Pen of the National Rally would beat him 70 percent to 30 percent in a run-off.

A peer-reviewed study from New York University Langone Health links exposure to Dinch, a plasticizer marketed as a safe alternative, to lower birth weight and fetal development complications, the Guardian reports. Dinch is widely used in soft plastic food packaging in the United States and European Union, and is found in children's toys, medical devices, some textiles and flooring.

Researchers analyzed federal US health data on more than 6,600 pregnancies from the National Institutes of Health's Echo program. Up to 70 percent of the women had Dinch in their urine. Higher levels raised the risk of a baby being classified as small for gestational age, meaning below the 10th percentile. Each tenfold increase in exposure was tied to a 27-gram reduction in birth weight; an average newborn weighs about 3,400 grams. Hispanic mothers and those with less education were more likely to have affected children. The authors say this is the first study to link Dinch to lower birth weight and length. They note that fetal growth problems can raise later risks of heart disease, learning difficulties and obesity.

Industry began shifting to Dinch after US and EU regulators acted against phthalates such as DEHP, describing it as a nontoxic, "high safety" option. The Guardian says global production rose from 25,000 tons in 2002 to 400,000 tons in 2024, and names BASF as a major producer. A response from producers was not included in the article.

The paper notes that animal and cell research suggests Dinch by-products can interfere with hormones guiding fetal development. The authors say little research exists on its health risks. Lead author Leonardo Trasande called for chemicals to be tested before they reach the market and pointed to the UN plastics treaty talks as a chance to set better policies.

The Food Packaging Forum, based in Switzerland, said it is concerned about the lack of health information. It noted evidence that Dinch migrates from packaging into food and that EU population levels have risen, and it is conducting its own research.

Ars Technica reports that scientists are still piecing together how Bantu speakers spread across much of Africa, one of history's largest and longest human migrations. The article says communities from western Africa began gradually expanding across the southern half of the continent starting 6,000 to 4,000 years ago. They brought farming, livestock, pottery-making and metalworking to regions previously dominated by hunter-gatherers.

Today around 350 million Africans speak one of roughly 500 Bantu languages, from Zulu to Swahili, and at least as many carry Bantu ancestry, according to the article. Researchers cite iron production at Great Zimbabwe, capital of a kingdom from 1000 to 1700 AD, as an example of the technology involved. Archaeometallurgist Ezekiel Mtetwa described the furnaces there as evidence of "intensive and technologically sophisticated iron production".

The idea of a migration began with language. Bantu tongues are so similar that a Portuguese crew member who had lived in west-central Africa could reportedly communicate with people in southeastern Africa in 1497. Archaeologists later found similar pottery, village life, metalwork, domesticated animals and western African crops across eastern and southern Africa, with northern sites generally older. By the 1990s some scholars asked whether these habits had spread without large movements of people.

Genetics helped settle that debate. A 2009 analysis of 2,432 Africans found Bantu speakers from western, central and southern Africa were more closely related than their geographic distance would suggest. A 2024 study of 1,763 genomes found the greatest diversity among Bantu speakers in western Africa, declining with distance, which coauthor Carina Schlebusch called a typical signature of expansion.

Gaps remain. Linguistic and genetic data point to the Grassfields region of Cameroon as the homeland, but conclusive archaeological proof is thin. Pottery at the Shum Laka rock shelter is a possible, yet inconclusive, trace of Bantu ancestors.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat, told Fox News Digital that he expects at least one House committee to investigate the Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, which was previously led by Elon Musk. "DOGE was a catastrophe for America, and at least one committee, I feel pretty certain, will investigate it," Raskin said, adding that he had "no specific plan."

Raskin also said "the whole thing was premised on a lie" and that Americans' private information was "completely compromised" by it. According to Fox, concern that DOGE allegedly had access to sensitive information is one reason calls for investigation have started. Fox described DOGE as launched at the start of President Donald Trump's second term to root out waste and make federal spending more transparent. Its efforts included deferred resignations and buyouts, and the federal workforce shrank by about 250,000 employees during 2025, according to the Government Accountability Office.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, also a Democrat, said there should be "a lot of inspection of what DOGE did" and called it "pretty awful." He was less certain about targeting Musk personally. "I don't know about focusing on one person," Pritzker said, and he added that he had never "heard anything like that" about a potential probe of Musk and DOGE.

Fox reported that Democrats in both chambers have vowed since the midterm elections to use investigative committees and subpoena powers to examine Musk, Trump and much of his administration, including efforts to impeach Trump. Some Democratic lawmakers have also suggested looking at the federal contracts held by Musk's companies and his role in cutting internet access to the Ukrainian military. The page text does not say which committee might act, and it does not include responses from Musk, DOGE or the White House.

At least a dozen California district attorneys, along with law enforcement unions, have publicly criticized Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute all 548 death sentences in the state, according to Fox News. Newsom announced the plan Thursday. It would convert the sentences to life without parole, though 382 cases still need approval from at least four California Supreme Court justices, according to the Associated Press.

In an open letter, Newsom wrote that he believes "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us." He issued a moratorium on executions on taking office in 2019, and California has not carried out one since 2006. His announcement says it does not repeal the death penalty. Fox said it asked his office for comment but did not hear back in time for publication. Anti-death penalty advocates praised the move, Fox reported.

Prosecutors argue it overrides juries and victims' families. Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho said justice requires "case-by-case consideration." San Bernardino County District Attorney Jason Anderson said he was not aware of any victims' relatives receiving notice and cited Marsy's Law, which protects victims' rights. Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer said recent parole regulations could put inmates "one step closer" to release. Newsom's office says the affected prisoners will remain in prison and are not eligible for release.

The prosecutors noted that voters rejected repeal initiatives in 2012 and 2016. Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman acknowledged the governor can commute sentences but said that power does not extend to eliminating the death penalty. San Diego County's Summer Stephan said her office was researching lawful remedies, and Kern County's Cynthia Zimmer said, "This assault on justice will be challenged."

Two heavily anticipated heart drugs have failed large clinical trials, with results presented Saturday at the American Heart Association meeting in Chicago. One targets lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), a cholesterol-carrying particle linked to heart attacks and strokes. The other targets inflammation.

In the Lp(a) study, led by Steven Nissen of the Cleveland Clinic, 8,350 adults with heart disease received either a placebo or Novartis's pelacarsen. According to NPR, the drug lowered Lp(a) by about 78%, but after five years that did not translate into fewer cardiovascular complications. "Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," Nissen said. Novartis, which sponsored the trial, said it "provides meaningful evidence" about Lp(a) and heart disease and may help inform future approaches.

Researchers offered several possible explanations, NPR reported. High Lp(a) might be a marker for something else rather than a cause. Treatment might need to last longer or start earlier. The trial might have needed participants with higher Lp(a), or people whose blood pressure and cholesterol were less well controlled. The problem might also lie with pelacarsen itself. Amgen and Eli Lilly are testing other Lp(a)-lowering drugs, with results expected over the next few years. UCLA cardiologist Karol Watson said, "The story's not over."

STAT reported that Novo Nordisk's ZEUS trial of the antibody ziltivekimab found that it reduced the inflammatory marker interleukin-6 but did not reduce heart attacks, strokes or deaths compared with placebo. Novo halted two other trials of the drug, HERMES and ATHENA, after a data monitoring committee found in September that they were unlikely to succeed. STAT's headline says cardiologists still plan to pursue anti-inflammatory treatments, but the rest of that article was behind a paywall and is not summarized here.

A report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR says AI is substantially speeding up research at Anthropic, according to The Verge. The report followed an 11-week investigation inside the company. It found Anthropic's models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little sign of slowing.

METR said benchmark scores suggest Anthropic made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year. Its researchers said they are confident the acceleration is not simply due to more computing power, and that most of it as of October "is due to AI." Employees using the company's most capable internal model reported being around 12 times as productive as they would be without AI, about double what staff reported a few months earlier. For now, METR said, much of the gain comes from AI assisting human researchers, though there are "some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon."

According to METR, Anthropic has finished training three models it has not released, codenamed Model 2, Model 3 and Model 4, completing training between July and October. METR also identified an unreleased model dating to 2022.

The Verge stressed the limits of the public report. Anthropic was allowed to redact it. METR wrote on X that it submitted a roughly 100-page report and that for the public version Anthropic "redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative." METR also said a small number of its data requests were denied, and that the public must rely on its judgment more than would be ideal. METR also said Anthropic shared more information than was initially scoped. The Verge noted the findings come as Anthropic prepares to go public. Anthropic's response to the redaction criticism was not included in the page text.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey Democrat helping write his party's artificial intelligence agenda, has disclosed new purchases of AI-linked stocks months after voting to ban lawmakers and their families from buying individual shares, according to CNBC. A filing released this week shows an October 12 purchase of between $1,001 and $15,000 of Benchmark Electronics stock. A jointly owned Morgan Stanley account also bought up to $15,000 of Applied Materials shares on October 26, after three earlier purchases of Advanced Micro Devices. CNBC said there is no evidence of wrongdoing.

Gottheimer's spokesman, Haraden Bottomley, said the congressman turned over control of his investments to a third party with "full investment discretion" before taking office in 2017. He said Gottheimer is awaiting congressional approval of a blind trust and has meanwhile set up an independent trust.

In July, Gottheimer was one of 13 Democrats who voted for the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would prohibit lawmakers and their families from buying most individual stocks. It passed the House but has not become law. CNBC noted some Democrats opposed it because it contained a voter-ID provision, and some said it did not go far enough.

The five trades totaled between $5,005 and $75,000, against disclosed household assets of $15.1 million to $59 million, CNBC reported. The purchases preceded a sharp selloff in AI stocks, with the Nasdaq Composite falling 5.5% Thursday. Benchmark closed at $59.34, roughly 25% below its price on the purchase date. The story comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January with new power to regulate and investigate the AI industry.

Tech companies face a growing run of child safety lawsuits even as they push AI tools into classrooms, CNBC reported. This week Snap confidentially settled a case alleging its technology caused severe psychological distress to two teenage users. Meta, TikTok and YouTube had previously settled with the plaintiffs in the same suit. Separately, Google was sued by the parents of a child who allegedly suffered a psychological crisis after chatting with the Gemini chatbot in Google Classroom.

The Snap settlement spared CEO Evan Spiegel from testifying in a Los Angeles court. Lawyer Joseph McNally called the settlements an effort by tech companies to "turn a corner" after reputational damage. A Snap spokesperson said the parties were pleased to resolve the matter. More trials are scheduled for March, and a federal case involving Meta, TikTok, Snap and YouTube, school districts and state attorneys general suits remains pending. In August, Meta agreed to pay nearly $17 billion to settle with a group of state attorneys general.

The Google suit alleges the company "hastily integrated" Gemini into school Chromebooks despite known risks. A Google spokesperson said it takes the claims seriously and has worked with medical professionals and academic experts on safeguards. The New York Times reported that schools that do not allow Google's AI tools for students will lose access to search; Google's Chris Phillips told the Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated."

Plaintiffs are focusing on product design rather than user content because of Section 230, CNBC noted, and OpenAI faces similar suits. Anthropic, which is planning to go public this month, highlighted the litigation issue in its prospectus.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani says cybercriminals have been publishing his personal data on the dark web, and Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has blamed pro-Russian hackers. Tajani wrote on X on Saturday that for days the hackers have been posting his data and seeking more, "effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation."

Tajani said the hackers are also targeting his family and are willing to pay for more details about him and his loved ones. "My response is very simple: I will not be intimidated in any way," he wrote. He did not specify the nature of the threats or what information had been shared, but suggested the cyberthreat was ongoing. He said Italy's position on Ukraine is the political reason he was targeted, and that taking a clear stand for a sovereign nation is "dangerous in the eyes of these criminal entities." Italy has given Ukraine humanitarian and military support.

Al Jazeera reported that Tajani also suggested the attacks might be a reaction to Italian efforts to strengthen the Foreign Ministry's digital defenses. He said the ministry was taking the threats seriously and coordinating its response with allied countries.

Meloni offered Tajani her "full solidarity." She called the sale of confidential information about officials "a cause of serious concern" that "must be tackled with the utmost determination," according to the BBC. She also voiced concern about "false images" that she said were shared by members of Italy's opposition, without describing them. Moscow has not publicly responded to the allegations, the BBC said. Al Jazeera noted the episode comes amid hoax bomb threats across Europe that have diverted flights.

A Guatemalan congressman and three police officers were killed in an armed attack on Friday, according to Guatemalan authorities, as reported by Al Jazeera. The attack targeted Julio Portillo, who was in the town of Rio Hondo in the eastern Zacapa department, an area known for drug trafficking activity.

Portillo was first taken to a hospital with serious injuries. His death was later confirmed by the National Unity of Hope party, known as UNE, to which he belonged. Guatemala's Congress said late Friday on X that its president, Luis Contreras, board members and lawmakers mourned the passing of Portillo, who represented the Zacapa district. President Bernardo Arevalo said the three National Civil Police officers died in the line of duty and told security forces to cooperate with prosecutors investigating the killings.

Authorities have not disclosed a motive or said who was responsible. Al Jazeera reported that the Lorenzana family cartel, which has links to Mexico's Sinaloa cartel, controls the drug trade in Zacapa. It did not link the group to the attack.
Portillo won his seat in 2023 for the opposition party Cabal but later switched to UNE, which is led by former First Lady Sandra Torres. She is expected to run for president in next year's elections.

The killings come about three weeks after former anticorruption prosecutor Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa was shot dead in Guatemala City, a case that raised concern about organized crime's influence and a possible return of politically motivated assassinations. Authorities have not established a connection between the two attacks.

Heavy rain and strong winds have flooded tents and threatened damaged buildings across Gaza, Al Jazeera reported. Water levels rose by 30 to 40 centimeters at several camps after Saturday's rain, and Gaza's civil defense agency received hundreds of calls.

In al-Mina camp in northern Gaza, where about 1,700 families live, Rana Adnan Hmeida said water soaked her family's bedding and clothes overnight. "My two-month-old baby was freezing," she said. Raed Abu Amsha said his tent collapsed on his family, including nine children in his care. In Nuseirat, Nasser al-Hajj lives in a tower block hit by an Israeli strike in September 2025. Water enters through a hole in his ceiling, and an engineer has warned him that more rubble could fall.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza live in areas exposed to flooding, and more than 400,000 are in areas at high risk. About 44,000 people are in structurally unsafe buildings, and more than 4,000 buildings are estimated to need full or partial demolition. About 294,250 families need shelter help ahead of winter, but available supplies cover only 18 percent of needs.

Gaza Municipality spokesperson Hosni Muhanna said about 15 kilometers of rainwater drainage lines and 212 kilometers of sewage networks are damaged, and eight pumping stations are out of service. The remaining system can handle no more than 20 percent of rainwater at best, he said. He added that shortages of fuel, equipment and spare parts limit repairs, and that more than 2,000 buildings in Gaza City are at risk of collapse. Emergency committees say tent and tarpaulin stocks fall far short of demand.

Six people were killed and about 15 injured in a shooting near the Main Market Square in Kraków, Poland, on Saturday, authorities said. Local police said on X that a man who drove into the square at about 3pm began "firing at random people from his car". Those killed were four women and two men.

Police said the gunman was a Polish citizen who acted alone. He wore military-style clothing and used a long military-type firearm. He was shot and wounded in a gunfight with officers nearby and was later taken to hospital, according to Al Jazeera. Two police officers were among the injured. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said one is in critical condition, and The Guardian reported that this officer was shot three times. The city's transport company said a tram driver reported being shot at near the square, which shattered his cabin window.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X that police are investigating the background and all circumstances of the attack. Government spokesperson Adam Szlapka said the event had shaken all of Poland and that Tusk was on his way to Kraków. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said the perpetrator would be held fully accountable. President Karol Nawrocki said he was deeply concerned. Condolences also came from EU diplomat Kaja Kallas, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the US ambassador to Poland, Tom Rose.

Kraków is Poland's second-largest city and a popular tourist destination. Al Jazeera said deadly shootings are extremely rare in Poland, though the country was already on high alert after a series of stabbings in October. The Guardian noted a Euronews report that legally owned firearms in Poland passed 1 million for the first time this year, with a record 50,700 gun permits issued in 2025. The pages do not give a motive.

New Zealand's general election on Saturday produced no clear winner, and the final shape of the next government may not be known for weeks. On preliminary results, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party is the largest party with 42 seats. The BBC and The Guardian both report that more than 99 percent of votes had been counted, with official results due on 27 November.

Together with coalition partners ACT (13 seats) and New Zealand First (12), National would hold a narrow lead over the left-leaning bloc, according to both outlets. The Guardian described that 67-seat majority as wafer thin and said the left bloc is three seats behind. It reported Labour on 35 seats; the BBC put Labour at 36. The Greens have 16, Te Pāti Māori five and the newcomer Opportunity Party seven. The Guardian said National edged Labour by 0.02 percent in the party vote.

Special votes, which include overseas ballots and those cast outside a voter's own electorate, are still to be counted. The Guardian said they tended to favour the left in 2023. Otago University election law expert Andrew Geddis said the outcome would come down to very fine margins.

Luxon said National has a pathway to forming a government and that caretaker conventions apply until final results. Labour leader Chris Hipkins did not concede, saying it may take longer to work out what voters have said. The Opportunity Party, which entered parliament for the first time, says it is open to working with either side but would negotiate first with the party that wins the most seats, the BBC reported.

Stephen Miller, who begins as White House chief of staff on Monday, pledged "absolute loyalty" to President Donald Trump in his first public remarks since the appointment, according to The Guardian. Speaking at an event on Friday evening, he called the job "the honor of my life" and promised "unwavering commitment" and "total devotion" to Trump's success. He previously served as deputy chief of staff and led the administration's immigration policy.

The move came days after Republicans suffered heavy midterm losses. The Guardian reported that Republicans lost seven Senate seats, 42 House seats and five governorships, and said JD Vance and others had blamed the Iran war and tariffs. Fox News reported that Democrats are on pace to win more than 250 House seats and at least 54 in the Senate.

Reaction among Republicans was divided. Indiana Representative Marlin Stutzman called the decision "horrible" and told Fox News that immigration positions had cost the party goodwill with Latino voters. Retiring Nebraska Representative Don Bacon said Miller had cost seats by alienating Hispanic voters. Fox reported that several House Republicans said Miller should be fired, while one lawmaker said Miller was not the reason the party lost.

The White House defended him. Spokeswoman Lauren Bis said Miller has been a key player in delivering Trump's agenda, and Vance and House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris praised the appointment. Trump called Miller one of his most trusted advisers. The Guardian said critics fear the administration will double down on its immigration agenda; the pages do not report Miller's plans for the role. Trump also told 60 Minutes he expects "a few changes" to his team.

Russia launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles at Ukraine overnight, hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and a bridge over the Dnipro, according to The Guardian. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of trying to "plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout".

Zelenskyy said the capital faced disruptions to electricity, water and heating, and that residential buildings, the Northern Bridge and a kindergarten were damaged. The Guardian reported five people injured in Kyiv, including a 14-year-old girl, while the BBC said nine people were reported hurt nationwide and that 12 regions came under attack. Strikes hit substations connecting the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine, and others in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Kyiv's water supply was operating normally again and about 60 percent of apartment buildings were connected to heating. Russia's defence ministry said it struck energy and transport targets.

Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the United States are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday. Zelenskyy said Moscow was preparing for those talks by attacking critical infrastructure. In a CNN interview he called a blueprint set out by Jared Kushner "Yalta 2.0". Kushner said discussions would cover a new European security framework and guarantees for Ukraine. President Donald Trump said a "big beautiful agreement" could be close. Zelenskyy said Russia must end the war first, with Ukraine given security guarantees.
Zelenskyy also appealed to the US Congress for increased bilateral support. The BBC noted that temperatures are dropping and parts of Ukraine have had their first winter snow.

Britain and France will lead the Coalition of the Willing's first major military exercise, a rehearsal for deploying a multinational force to Ukraine after the war ends, according to Defense News. The exercise, KOALICJA 26.2, runs from Nov. 9 to 22 and brings together 2,800 troops from 11 nations for activities in Poland, France and Turkey under the coalition's Multinational Force-Ukraine (MNF-U). American troops will not take part.

The British Ministry of Defence said the drills combine air, land and sea forces to test how to move, protect and supply a force that would help rebuild Ukraine's armed forces once fighting ends. They will also test command-and-control arrangements. Britain is sending 300 personnel, France is sending hundreds, including a unit with about 50 contact drones, and nearly 2,000 Polish soldiers will participate. Turkey will not send troops to Poland but will stand up the force's maritime element in Istanbul to test mine clearance, so commercial shipping can return to Ukraine's ports.

The French ministry said the force's possible missions include securing critical infrastructure, training Ukraine's military, helping protect the skies and clearing Black Sea mines. The force reportedly will not have a peacekeeping or ceasefire-monitoring mandate or operate under NATO command, and would enter Ukraine only after a ceasefire and at Kyiv's request.

The announcements do not give the final size of a deployment. Britain and France said earlier this year they were prepared to contribute roughly 5,000 troops each. Russian President Vladimir Putin has rejected any foreign troop presence in Ukraine. The exercise comes as US, Russian and Ukrainian negotiators are set to meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps says it is building underground military complexes able to keep producing and storing weapons under heavy bombardment, Al Jazeera reported. IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi told a Tehran news conference on Saturday that missile and drone production lines had been moved underground, and that an "underground missile city" is due to be unveiled, according to Iranian media. He said this let Iran keep producing while adversaries assumed its stockpiles were dwindling. He also warned that restrictions on the range of Iranian missiles had been lifted.

The claims come amid a war that the US and Israel launched against Iran on February 28. Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, triggering a global energy crisis. President Donald Trump said on Friday that US forces carried out limited strikes on Qeshm Island and that talks with Iran had made "a lot of progress". The US also maintains a naval blockade on Iran and has added sanctions.

Separately, The Guardian reported that Qatar, the lead mediator, is urging Tehran to let UN nuclear inspectors visit its bombed nuclear sites. Under the proposal, the US would lift the blockade and release part of Iran's $8bn in frozen assets, and Iran would reopen the strait on the second day via a route negotiated with Oman. Iran would not have to commit to removing its enriched uranium stockpile. Qatar's emir spoke with Trump about the plan, his office said, without giving details.

Iran has listed other preconditions, including an end to the war in Lebanon, US withdrawal from its coastline and war reparations. It has also said it distrusts IAEA chief Rafael Grossi. The Guardian said sequencing of the steps is at the heart of the mediation.

Iraq has evidence that outside parties have used its territory to launch attacks on neighbouring countries, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein told Al Jazeera in an interview on Saturday. He said Baghdad is investigating attacks on Gulf states launched from Iraqi soil and is trying to resolve disagreements with Saudi Arabia through dialogue.

Saudi Arabia has accused Iran-aligned groups in Iraq of attacking its oil infrastructure. In September, Baghdad confirmed that drone attacks on the kingdom's East-West pipeline came from Iraqi territory. Hussein said Iraq is negotiating with Iran-aligned armed factions to bring their weapons under state control, and that this must be done through dialogue rather than force. He said Iraq is also in contact with Tehran about the weapons the factions hold.

The government had set a September 30 deadline for factions to hand over weapons, the date the US-led coalition against ISIL was due to end its mandate and leave Iraq. After meeting resistance, it pushed the deadline back to June 2027, despite long-standing US pressure on disarmament, Al Jazeera reported.

On balancing relations with Tehran and Washington, Hussein confirmed that the US had formally asked Iraq to close all but two of its border crossings with Iran. He said Iraq welcomes friendship with Iran but rejects interference in its internal affairs. He also said Iraq lost about $60bn when oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz were suspended, though shipments have resumed after understandings with Washington and Tehran. Iraq, Syria, Jordan and Turkiye have formed a committee to fight ISIL's presence in Syria, he said.

Democratic socialists won a series of offices in Tuesday's elections. In Los Angeles, city councilwoman Nithya Raman, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, according to both The Guardian and Fox News. Fox reported that DSA member Janeese Lewis George also won the mayoralty in Washington, D.C.

The two outlets frame the results differently. The Guardian said Raman's win means America's two largest cities, Los Angeles and New York, will be run by democratic socialist mayors. Fox counted four of the 20 largest US cities with socialist leaders, adding Washington, Seattle's Katie Wilson and New York's Zohran Mamdani, and estimated about 44 million people live in those metro areas. Heritage Foundation fellow Mike Gonzalez, quoted by Fox, criticized the trend, and Fox cited polls showing 32 percent of voters view socialism favorably.

The Guardian reported that the Los Angeles chapter, DSA-LA, had its largest-ever slate of wins. Marissa Roy won city attorney with 67.39 percent, and Angela Gonzales-Torres beat Representative Jimmy Gomez, who was backed by AIPAC, with 60.6 percent. Burbank gained what the chapter called the first socialist-majority city council on the west coast. Volunteers knocked on more than 110,000 doors. Fox said seven DSA-backed or affiliated candidates won House seats nationally.

The Guardian said Bass was deeply unpopular and that frustration over her handling of the Palisades fire hurt her, according to UCLA's Zev Yaroslavsky. It also noted the chapter's endorsement of Raman was contested internally. Raman takes office in December, Fox reported.
